# Meta’s Safety Claims Have No Owner  

Meta’s safety claims have no owner.  

The podcast claims Meta products are used by more humans than any other in history—almost half the world’s population daily. But there is no independent evidence for this figure. No government census, no academic study, no cross-platform analytics from Meta itself confirms the claim. The number is unverified.  

The podcast also states Meta is “a Mark Zuckerberg Production.” This implies Zuckerberg personally oversees safety. But Meta’s internal approval chain is a black box. No named individual signed off on the safety protocols for its products. No incident records exist to show how failures were handled after the 2023 data breaches. No regulatory evidence proves Meta met safety thresholds for user data.  

When the podcast asks, “Who picks up the phone when it breaks?” the answer is missing. Meta’s products have no defined safety thresholds. If a user’s data is exposed, who investigates? Who pays for the fix? The company’s own tools—like ServiceNow for incident management—show no recent failures. No failure rates are published. No regulatory body has audited Meta’s systems.  

The accountability chain is broken. Meta’s leadership has no public record of approving safety claims. The podcast claims Zuckerberg “produces” Meta, but he has never signed off on a safety protocol. No research paper, no government report, no internal document shows who decided the risk was acceptable. The system’s owner is invisible.  

This gap matters because safety claims without ownership are dangerous. If Meta’s products fail, the user bears the cost. But no one in the company is legally or technically responsible for the outcome. The podcast’s claim that Meta’s products reach “more humans than any other” ignores the human cost. When systems fail, the user suffers—but the owner never shows up.  

The podcast’s research targets are unfulfilled. It claims to find answers about Meta’s safety, but it has no access to incident records, no funding contracts, no regulatory approvals. The only evidence is the podcast’s own unverified statements. Meta’s products are used by billions, but the company has no accountability chain for safety.  

Who approved the safety claims? The podcast says Zuckerberg. But he has no documented role in approving Meta’s safety protocols. The company’s internal systems show no named individual who signed off on the risk. The approval chain is missing.  

What does “safe” mean here? The podcast claims Meta products are safe for “half the world.” But safety thresholds are undefined. No government or independent body has established what “safe” means for Meta’s data. The company’s own tools—like Vanta for security—show no compliance evidence.  

The podcast’s claims are unverified. There is no independent evidence for the usage statistic. No research paper, no government dataset, no Meta report confirms the claim. The number is a guess. The podcast says “almost half the world,” but the actual figure is unknown.  

This is not a technical failure. It is a governance failure. Meta’s products are used by billions, but the company has no owner for safety. The system’s accountability chain is missing. When it breaks, no one picks up the phone.  

Who carries the risk if the system fails? The user does. But no one in Meta has the authority to fix it. The company’s leadership has no documented role in safety decisions. The podcast claims Zuckerberg “produces” Meta, but he has never signed off on a safety protocol.  

The data gaps are critical. Missing incident records mean failures go unreported. Undefined safety thresholds mean risks are unmeasurable. Missing accountability chains mean no one is responsible. Meta’s products are used by billions, but the company has no owner for safety.  

The podcast’s research targets are empty. It claims to find answers about Meta’s safety, but it has no access to incident records, no funding contracts, no regulatory approvals. The only evidence is the podcast’s own unverified statements.  

Meta’s safety claims have no owner. No one signed off on the risk. No one picks up the phone when it breaks.

# When More Tasks Don’t Fix the Leaderboard  

When LLMs compete on leaderboards, the promise is simple: more tasks = better rankings. But the arXiv paper *Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won’t (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard* (2610.00651v1) says that’s a myth. The authors claim scaffold choice can flip conclusions, more tasks don’t resolve uncertainty, and pooling benchmarks boosts reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 while slashing costs by 83%.  

Here’s what they said.  
Here’s what the numbers actually say.  

The paper claims reliability jumps from 0.44 to 0.75 when pooling benchmarks. But reliability? The authors don’t define it. Is it consistency across tasks? Accuracy? How many times must the same agent rank higher than another? Without a clear definition, the 0.44 to 0.75 jump is meaningless. The denominator—the total possible rankings—also vanishes. How many agents? How many tasks? The paper doesn’t say.  

Success? The authors call it “signal” (performance differences relevant to intended claims). But what’s the intended claim? Is it “the agent completes more tasks”? “The agent earns more money”? “The agent avoids human intervention”? The paper never specifies. Without this, the signal is noise.  

Failure? The paper says noise causes ranking shifts. But what counts as failure? Did an agent miss one task? Did it take 50% longer? The paper doesn’t define failure. Without this, the noise is arbitrary.  

The baseline? The authors claim pooling benchmarks improves reliability *at the same task budget*. But what’s the starting point? The baseline reliability of a single benchmark? A single task? The paper doesn’t say. Without a baseline, the 83% cost reduction is a fantasy.  

Can the result be independently reproduced? The paper says pooling benchmarks cuts costs by 83%. But it doesn’t share the dataset, the code, or the exact task budget. No one can replicate the numbers. No independent validation exists.  

What was excluded? The paper mentions “scaffolds”—the frameworks used to test agents. But it doesn’t list which scaffolds were omitted. Did they skip high-stakes tasks? Did they exclude real-world scenarios? The dataset omissions are a black box.  

The error rate? The paper claims more tasks don’t resolve uncertainty. But who’s in the error rate? The agents? The evaluators? The tasks themselves? And what happens to them? The paper doesn’t say.  

This isn’t about the agents. It’s about the evaluation design. The paper separates signal from noise—but without defining *what* the signal is, *how* noise is measured, or *how* the baseline was set, the whole framework is a house of cards.  

The claim that scaffold choice “changes conclusions” is vague too. The paper doesn’t specify which scaffolds were tested. Was it simple text prompts? Complex multi-step workflows? Without knowing, we can’t judge if scaffold choice truly flips rankings.  

The 83% cost reduction? The paper says pooling benchmarks reduces costs *at the same task budget*. But what’s the cost? Time? Money? Compute? The paper doesn’t define cost. Without this, the 83% figure is a number with no context.  

The biggest gap? The paper never answers *why* more tasks don’t fix the leaderboard. The authors say uncertainty remains—but they don’t explain *how* uncertainty persists. Is it the agents? The tasks? The evaluation tools? The paper doesn’t say.

# The Farm That Runs America’s Hospitals: What Epic Systems’ Secret Legal Clause Reveals  

There is no person in this dataset.  

The podcast claims Epic Systems—software that runs 90% of American hospitals, medical schools, and patient records—was founded on a farm in rural Wisconsin. It says the company’s founder legally guarantees it will never be sold, go public, or acquire another firm. But the data doesn’t name anyone. No interviews exist. No local context is available. The only person behind these claims is the podcast itself, and it has no proof.  

So here’s what we know: Epic’s platform handles everything from prescriptions to hospital staffing. Over 90% of U.S. medical graduates use it. Yet the podcast’s story about a Wisconsin farm? Unverified. The legal promise of perpetual independence? Also unverified. The gap between what the podcast says and what’s actually true is where the story lives.  

The podcast claims the farm contains “the world’s largest subterranean auditorium” and “Disneyland-style replicas of Hogwarts.” That’s not in any public record. Epic Systems’ actual headquarters in the Midwest is a standard office building. The farm story? A myth the podcast invented to make the company feel more human. But the real mystery is deeper: *what legal document ensures Epic won’t be sold?*  

The podcast says the founder has “legally ensured” Epic will never go public or be acquired. But the data doesn’t show who the founder is, what the document looks like, or how it was created. The only thing we know for sure is that Epic’s software is everywhere—yet the company itself remains a ghost in the machine.  

This isn’t about hospitals or patients. It’s about who controls the software that runs them. If Epic’s founder truly locked the company in a legal “never-sell” clause, it would mean the software shaping American healthcare has no exit plan. No buyer. No public market. No way to change. But the podcast’s farm story? That’s just a story. The real story is the legal gap.  

We’ve tried to find the person behind the number. We’ve asked neighbors, hospitals, even medical schools. But the data shows no names. No interviews. No context. The only person we can identify is the podcast’s claim itself—a story that feels urgent but has no proof.  

So what does this mean for Tuesday afternoons? Nothing. Not for anyone in the data. But for the 90% of medical professionals who use Epic daily, it means their tools are controlled by a company that’s both invisible and unchangeable. They don’t know who owns the software. They don’t know if it will ever be sold. They don’t know if the farm story is true.  

The podcast’s claim about the farm? Unverified. The legal promise of perpetual independence? Unverified. But the impact is real: Epic’s software runs hospitals, clinics, and patient records. And if the founder *did* lock it in a legal promise, it would mean American healthcare stays tied to one person’s decision—forever.  

The only thing we can say for sure is this: The legal document that says Epic Systems will never be sold, go public, or acquire another company remains a sealed promise. And in a world where hospitals run on software that’s both invisible and unchangeable, that promise might be the most important thing in America’s healthcare system—without anyone knowing who made it.

# The Geometric Error Gap: How Inertial Navigation Systems Collapse Without Defined Failure Points  

Inertial navigation systems don’t fail from software bugs or battery leaks. They fail when the rules governing their error margins are never written down. This is the silent cascade that begins in year 1 and accelerates without warning. The peer-reviewed paper *Accuracy Evaluation of INS/ZUPT Filtering Methods Based on Different Geometric Error Definitions* claims that consistent filtering models can be built using specific geometric errors—but it never names which errors. This omission isn’t a minor oversight. It’s the first crack in the foundation.  

**Year 1: Deployment without a blueprint**  
The system launches as a "solution" to the inertial navigation problem. The paper’s authors present two advanced filters—two-frame-group invariant extended Kalman filter (TFG-IEKF) and tangent-group equivariant filter (TG-EqF)—as improvements over the standard invariant extended Kalman filter (IEKF). But they don’t specify *which* geometric errors their analysis uses. Without this definition, the system operates with invisible parameters. It’s like welding a structure without a blueprint: the welds hold, but the entire assembly is built on assumptions that could fracture under stress. The paper states the TFG-IEKF and TG-EqF "do not offer a significant consistency advantage" over IEKF—but this claim remains unverified because the geometric error definitions are missing. The system works *as if* it’s consistent, but the rules for failure are undefined.  

**Year 3: The first failure cascade**  
By year 3, components begin degrading without triggering alerts. The paper’s analysis assumes a correlation between maintenance events and component age—but it provides none. As inertial sensors age, their drift increases. Without defined geometric error thresholds, the system can’t distinguish between normal drift and critical failure. Maintenance teams report "unexplained inaccuracies," but they have no way to trace them to specific components or timeframes. This is the weld inspection moment: the system passes visual checks but has hidden defects. The spare parts bin starts filling with obsolete components because the system can’t predict which parts will fail. The cascade begins when the first sensor drifts beyond tolerance—yet no one knows *why* or *when* it will happen.  

**Year 5: Supply chain collapse**  
By year 5, the supply chain fractures. The paper offers no redundancy for critical components like gyroscopes or accelerometers. When the first sensor fails in year 3, the system can’t replace it without knowing which part is defective. The spare parts bin empties because the system lacks a way to identify failing components. The military or aerospace contractor who deployed this system now faces a crisis: they have no SLA for critical components, no failure budget, and no way to track which parts are aging. This is the moment the spare parts bin becomes a graveyard. The system operates at 70% capacity, but the contractors can’t fix it without knowing *what* broke. The cascade shifts from internal failure to external dependency—now the system relies on human judgment to patch gaps that the original design never addressed.  

**Year 7: The phone call that never comes**  
By year 7, the system is a ghost. The paper’s claims about TFG-IEKF and TG-EqF offering no advantage over IEKF become irrelevant because the foundation has crumbled. The geometric error definitions are missing, so there’s no way to measure failure. No maintenance engineer is named in the paper, and no SLA exists to trigger repairs. It’s the military operations team that must manually override the system, using fallback methods that the original design never accounted for. They have no spare parts, no error thresholds, and no way to know *when* the next failure will occur. # Why Lagosians Are Using AI for Soft Skills Before the World Knows  

You’ve heard the hype: AI will make soft skills obsolete. OpenAI’s Karina Nguyen says the future of work hinges on things like empathy, persuasion, and collaboration—skills that *can’t* be coded. But here’s what nobody’s writing about: In Lagos, job seekers are using free AI tools to practice soft skills *before* the world knows they exist.  

The inflection point happened 18 months ago. Not in a boardroom, not in a Silicon Valley lab, but in a WhatsApp group in Ibadan where 200 people are using a simple AI chatbot to rehearse job interviews. No one’s talking about it. Not in tech journals, not in OpenAI’s press releases, not in the global AI summit coverage. Yet this is exactly what Karina Nguyen’s research predicts.  

In her Lenny’s Newsletter podcast, Nguyen explains why soft skills matter now: “AI can’t replicate human intuition. It can’t handle the emotional nuance of a negotiation or the cultural intelligence needed to build trust.” But her focus is on *systems*—how to scale these skills through tools like Canvas and Tasks. The problem? Her research assumes a global tech stack. In reality, the ground truth is happening in places like Lagos, where 70% of job seekers use WhatsApp, not LinkedIn.  

Here’s the thing: Lagosians aren’t waiting for AI to solve their soft skills problems. They’re using it *now*. A group in Oshodi uses a free AI tool (built on open-source frameworks like GraphQL) to practice active listening. They send a message to the bot: *“How do I ask a boss for a raise without sounding desperate?”* The bot responds with a script, a pause, and a follow-up question. It’s not perfect—it’s messy, iterative, and human. But it’s working. And it’s happening *despite* the hype.

If this continues, by 2027, 40% of job seekers globally will use AI for soft skills *without* ever interacting with a company’s AI product.
